tweets.text: I don’t normally do things like this, but we’ll see what happens. $AAOI

$AAOI — my notes on tonight’s earnings AAOI reports Q2 after the US close tonight. But the numbers that matter in this report aren’t the Q2 numbers. In Q1 the company did $151.1 million in revenue, up 51% year over year. Data center jumped to $81.4 million, CATV stayed at $66.8 million. Gross margin came in at 29.2%, down from 31.4% in Q4 2025. Non-GAAP loss of 7 cents per share. Guidance for Q2 is $180-198 million, 29-30% margin, EPS between -$0.03 and +$0.03. Consensus sits near $190 million in revenue and 2 cents of profit. The market is pricing in the first profitable quarter in over two years. So far the story is clean. The real issue is the arithmetic. Management is targeting over $1.1 billion in revenue and over $140 million in operating income for 2026. Using the midpoint of Q2 guidance, the first half comes to roughly $340 million. That leaves $760 million for the rest of the year — Q3 and Q4 each need to be nearly double Q2. The operating income side is harsher: if the first half closes around breakeven, the entire $140 million has to come from the second half. That implies roughly an 18% operating margin in H2, a level this company hasn’t seen in recent history. That’s why I’ll be watching the Q3 guidance tonight, not the Q2 print. If Q3 doesn’t come in somewhere around $280-350 million, the full-year target starts to break mathematically. The second thing I’m watching is capacity. By management’s own words, the constraint is production, not demand. They exited Q1 at 100,000 units a month of 800G/1.6T capacity, targeting 150,000 in Q2 and over 650,000 by year end. The new Texas facility comes online in Q3/Q4, and 1.6T shipments start late in Q3. Any slip in that timeline pushes the revenue target with it. Third is product mix. 800G revenue was only $4.6 million in Q1, 5.6% of data center sales. Getting margins above 29% depends on that share growing. Management talks about 40% long term — I want to see the first concrete evidence of it this quarter. The risks are clear. Customer concentration is extreme: one CATV customer at 44% of revenue, two data center customers at 26% and 25%, and the top 10 at 98%. The $600 million ATM program opened in May carries dilution risk. CapEx is climbing fast. Finally, the FCC news. On Tuesday Reuters reported a ban being drafted on imports of new Chinese optical transceivers, and the stock jumped 16%. But scale matters here: AAOI did $81 million in datacom revenue in Q1 against Innolight’s $2.6 billion. AAOI can’t fill that gap. This news expands the multiple, not near-term revenue. The stock has come from $233 in May down to around $127, with a beta of 2.29. The expectation bar is high and the margin for error is thin.

$AAOI From 2017 to 2023, the company was essentially stagnant. Revenue bottomed out at $190.9M in 2019 and was still only $217.6M by 2023. In other words, there was little meaningful growth over a six-year period. Then demand for optical interconnects used in AI data centers took off. Revenue reached $455.7M in 2025, representing 82.8% year-over-year growth. The real story, however, lies in expectations. Revenue for 2026 is projected at $1.03B, more than double the 2025 figure. For the following year, expectations rise to $2.57B. In other words, the market is pricing in a roughly fivefold increase in revenue over just two years. This is where investors need to be cautious. When expectations like these are already reflected in the stock price, even a single quarter of execution delays or the loss of a major customer can trigger a sharp market reaction. The higher the expectations, the narrower the margin for error.
